1. The animation shows a grid of squares. Each square stands for a historical scenario, probably a different starting period. A light square means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark square means the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The frames are labeled "illustrative," "US only" and "history, not a forecast." The idea is that buying beat renting in most historical ten-year windows, but not in all of them.

2. The grid barely changes. Only the text overlays change. Frame 1 has no caption. Frames 2 to 4 add "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%." Frames 5 and 6 add "the share moves with the rent you assume." The captions also shift position slightly. The dark column of renter-ahead squares stays in the same place.

3. If rents are assumed to grow about 6% a year, the buyer came out ahead in about 92.2% of the historical cases. The result depends on the rent assumption. A different rent growth figure would change the share of light and dark squares.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually won over ten-year stretches in the past. They might also take away that this depends on assumptions and isn't guaranteed. The "history, not a forecast" label warns against treating it as a prediction.

5. The takeaway about buying usually winning comes from the on-screen text and the mostly light grid. The caution that the result depends on assumptions is also on screen. Any actual advice, such as "you should buy," would be my own conclusion, because the animation doesn't say that.
